title: When you make your AI game, how is it presented to you?
author: ZorKlag456
selftext:
Is it an executable file you can download, is it something you open up in your game engine?

What's the way?

replies.author: ZorKlag456
replies.body: When you give a gpt a prompt to make a game for you, do you just download it and run it?

replies.author: WillowKisz
replies.body: Yes and then you earn. Repeat 1000x for maximum profit

replies.author: ZorKlag456
replies.body: I'm not sure it's going to be that easy to profit from it but if it works for you then good on you.

comments.author: Wow_Crazy_Leroy_WTF
comments.body:
I think there’s more than one way to skin this cat.  For example, it could be Java script /HTML game that you open and play on your browser. (You may have to copy and paste the code into a TXT file with the right extension as opposed to just downloading it)

On the high end, there could be an EXE file connected to many folders and files but GPT is not gonna just spit it out for you. You need Codex to work inside your directory with all the moving parts.

comments.author: MysteriousPepper8908
comments.body: Like the other comments have said, it depends. If it's HTML/Javascript, most LLMs have a built in compiler that lets you play the game in the chat window but if you want to use it separately, you'll need to download the file and run it in your browser or potentially run it in a compiler if it's something like Python. When you get to start doing more advanced stuff, you're likely going to want an engine like Unreal Engine or Unity and in that case, the AI isn't really building a whole game for you, it's building scripts which you can attach to objects to make certain things happen which you can then play in the editor or export to an executable for various platforms. By default, the LLM will tell you the setup, what sort of object you need to set up and how to implement the script but it's more of an involved process at that point.

comments.author: Cool-Chemical-5629
comments.body: It's never an executable file in traditional sense (as in .exe file). However, the direct output usually can be used in preparation of what you would normally do as a programmer to build the exe file. As someone else mentioned here, if you wanted the AI to help you all the way to exe file creation, you would need an AI agent with access to your files in your system. Basically, you would be using the AI to control your PC through console commands which may be enough for it to help you compile the game into the final exe form. But then again, it depends on what kind of format would you expect. Obviously if it is a web browser game that runs somewhere on the server, you would not need an exe file.

comments.author: morewordsfaster
comments.body:
It depends on what AI tools you use and what you prompt the AI to produce. If you're using something like Google AI Studio, it's going to build a TypeScript+React or TypeScript+Angular project that can be deployed to the web.

If you want to do something using Godot, Unity, or Unreal, you'll need something like Cursor or Claude and either an MCP server so the agent can use the engine to create the game, or you'll be the agent's eyes and hands completing its instructions in the engine to pair up with code that it produces. When you're done you'll be able to build an executable for mobile or PC or web or whatever.

If you prefer a code-heavy approach you could use an AI IDE and build a project using raylib and whichever language bindings you want. You won't have a game/level editor with this approach, but you may not need one .

comments.author: lordpoee
comments.body: Usually, I build all my functions and features, kind of like a code lego kit, then I get it all arranged in my Notepad++ and compile.

comments.author: lordpoee
comments.body:
do this buddy,  
type  
"Generate code for simple html5 asteroid style game."  
copy the code, save as html and open in browser,  
if it's not working hit f12, copy the error and send it back to the AI  
This will get you started but I haven't met an AI that will really produce "whole game", you need to prompt it to build additional functions and features.
